It seems like for display holography, edge lit would be the way to go. For a potential customer, no additional light would be needed. Just hang the hologram on the wall and plug it in. I have read all three techniques in Saxby's book.

posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md:
One of the main reasons why holography hasn't gone anywhere is because of the complications involved with lighting them. Another thing holding holography back is the typically atrocious subject matter. Yet another thing is the revolting monochromaticity of many of them (such as that awful, familiar green). Achromatic or broadband is fine, or subtle true-color using two or more lasers (but definitely not awful, exaggerated pseudocolor techniques).

Personally I try to step back and take a look at the problem as a whole. As for the holograms I intend to make, I have looked at all the factors going into making them, and haved developed my own approach, including the lighting technique. I'm not going into details because everyone has their own "goals" and if just one of these "goals" changes, it can have huge repercussions, affecting every part of the system. For example, my system involves split-beam holography, and this is necessary for the kind of built-in reconstructing light I want to use. (Not many people seem to be interested in split-beam holography.)

But beyond all this, holography will only come into its own when people want to buy holograms not because they are holograms, but in spite of being holograms. Since people will probably not agree with this, I don't see much point in discussing it further.

The last edge lit hologram I recall seeing was at the International Symposium on Display Holography in 2000 in Austria. Ryder Nesbitt did it as his thesis project at MIT, which published plenty of papers on the technique in the '80's through 90's.

It looked like one would expect, and image plane coming out of the plexi block, which was pretty thick, like 20 to 25 mm. The bulb was in the base.

A guy named Mike Mertz, Merz, or Metz claimed to have a patent on the technique, so some people kind of shied away from the technology. I must have seen other samples of the edge lit business, but nothing pops into my mind's eye.

But right now, this very moment, you just might be looking at an edge lit hologram, if you are viewing a laptop! Think of the thorny problem of evenly illuminating a 10" by 12" rectangle from an edge. I kind of think that there is some sort of holographic diffuser that provides the very even backlighting for the LCD screen. Anybody ever take apart a dead laptop to check out the optics for illuminating the screen?

I searched and I had the paper. Here it is.http://www.holograms3d.com/Papers/Deep% ... ograms.pdfNow I am thinking, if this technique could be combined with the edge light hologram then a very easy way of illuminating the edge lit hologram can be done using one of those long tube lights found in a laptop screen.

I don't know if that would be doable. But I recall edge lits to have some special features: edge lit transmission holograms show less dispersion than “normal” transmission holograms do. In contrast edge lit reflection holograms have much more dispersion than “normal” reflection holograms.

So in order to get little image blur in an edge lit reflection hologram, you need rather thick layers (30um or so). That limits the choice of recording materials. Silver halides may be out in that case. And DCG might also turn out to be unfit for edge lit. Photopolymers might be a better choice. 

Moreover, there's the serious problem of matching the index of refraction of the glass/plastic block with that of the recording material...
